title: WHY DID GOD TOLERATE POLYGAMY IF GENESIS PRESENTS ONE MAN AND ONE WOMAN?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD TOLERATE POLYGAMY IF GENESIS PRESENTS ONE MAN AND ONE WOMAN?
The Bible Records Men With Multiple Wives—So Why Did God Allow Something That Was Never His Original Design?
There is a question hiding in the pages of the Old Testament that many Christians have wondered about but are sometimes afraid to ask.
If God's design for marriage was one man and one woman...
why did Abraham have more than one woman in his household?
Why did Jacob marry Leah and Rachel?
Why did David have multiple wives?
Why did Solomon have hundreds?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all...
Why didn't God immediately stop them?
Read that question carefully.
Because there is an enormous difference between asking, “Does the Bible contain polygamy?” and asking, “Does the Bible present polygamy as God's ideal?”
Those are not the same question.
And confusing them can make Scripture appear to contradict itself when, in reality, something much deeper is happening.
The Bible is brutally honest about humanity.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not erase their dysfunctional families.
It does not hide their compromises so that religious people can feel more comfortable.
Scripture will tell you that a man trusted God...
and then tell you where that same man failed.
It will show you David worshiping...
and David sinning.
Solomon asking God for wisdom...
and Solomon later behaving foolishly.
Jacob receiving God's promises...
while living inside a household fractured by rivalry.
Why?
Because the Bible isn't primarily the story of good people becoming impressive.
It is the story of a holy God pursuing sinful people who desperately need redemption.
And that distinction changes everything.
Before Abraham...
before Jacob...
before David...
before Solomon...
before Israel had kings...
before Moses gave Israel civil regulations for life in a fallen society...
there was Eden.
And Eden matters.
Because when Jesus was questioned about marriage centuries later, He did something extraordinary.
He went backward.
Back beyond Moses.
Back beyond Israel.
Back beyond the patriarchs.
Back to the beginning.
Genesis 2:24 says in Hebrew:
עַל־כֵּן֙ יַֽעֲזָב־אִ֔ישׁ אֶת־אָבִ֖יו וְאֶת־אִמּ֑וֹ וְדָבַ֣ק בְּאִשְׁתּ֔וֹ וְהָי֖וּ לְבָשָׂ֥ר אֶחָֽד׃
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew is beautiful.
וְדָבַק — wəḏāḇaq — carries the idea of clinging, holding fast, being joined.
בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ — bə’ištô — “to his wife.”
And then:
לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד — ləḇāśār ’eḥāḏ.
“One flesh.”
One covenant union.
The text does not introduce Adam and a collection of wives.

God forms the woman and brings her to the man, and Genesis describes the resulting covenant pattern as the man holding fast to “his wife” and the two becoming one flesh. The Hebrew text itself preserves that movement toward covenantal unity.
And Jesus deliberately returns to that beginning.
That is crucial.
When discussing marriage in Matthew 19, Jesus appeals to creation and says that the Creator made them male and female, then quotes Genesis 2:24 and speaks of the two becoming one flesh.
In other words, Jesus does not look at every marital arrangement recorded in Israel's history and say, “Whatever happened historically must therefore be the ideal.”
He goes back to creation.
That gives us a vital principle for reading the entire Bible:
Description is not automatically prescription.
The Bible describing something does not necessarily mean God is endorsing it.
Cain murders Abel.
Scripture records it.
It does not endorse murder.
Abraham lies.
Scripture records it.
It does not endorse lying.
David commits adultery.
Scripture records it.
It does not endorse adultery.
Solomon accumulates wives.
Scripture records it.
That does not automatically turn Solomon's household into God's blueprint for marriage.
This is where the question becomes more interesting.
Because someone may respond:
“But God didn't merely record polygamy. The Law actually contains regulations dealing with households involving more than one wife.”
Correct.
And that is precisely where we must distinguish regulation from approval.

Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses a situation involving two wives and protects the inheritance rights of the firstborn son when one woman is preferred over another. Whatever interpretive questions surround the precise household situation, the command's concern is unmistakable: personal favoritism must not be allowed to rob the rightful firstborn of his inheritance.
Exodus 21:10 likewise regulates obligations toward a woman when another wife is taken, insisting that her provision and marital rights not simply be discarded.
God is dealing with real people in a real fallen society.
And sometimes biblical law restrains the damage caused by human sin without presenting the damaged situation itself as the creation ideal.
Think about that.
A law regulating the consequences of something is not necessarily a celebration of that thing.

There is an enormous difference between God saying, “This is My beautiful design,” and God saying, in effect, “Since you are living in this broken reality, you may not use that reality as permission to exploit another human being.”
Jesus gives us an interpretive category for this when discussing divorce.
His words in Matthew 19:8 are devastating:
πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν
pros tēn sklērokardian hymōn
“because of your hardness of heart.”
Then Jesus says:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως.
“But from the beginning it was not so.”
There it is.
The distinction between what God permits within human brokenness and what God established “from the beginning.”
Jesus was speaking specifically about Mosaic permission concerning divorce, so we should not carelessly pretend that this verse directly says, “Moses permitted polygamy because of hardness of heart.”
It doesn't.
Biblical faithfulness requires us to say exactly what the text says.
But Jesus gives us an important theological category: some Mosaic provisions address fallen human realities without redefining the Creator's original design.
And when you look at the Old Testament's actual portrayal of polygamous households...
the supposed glamour disappears very quickly.
Look at Abraham's household.
Sarah cannot conceive.
Hagar enters the situation.
A child is conceived.
And almost immediately the house fills with contempt, jealousy, bitterness and pain.
Hagar suffers.
Sarah suffers.
Abraham is caught in the middle.
Ishmael eventually leaves with his mother.
Whatever someone thinks polygamy promises, Genesis does not paint this household like a romantic advertisement.
Then comes Jacob.
Jacob loves Rachel.
Laban deceives him into marrying Leah.
Jacob later marries Rachel as well.
And what follows?
Competition.
Comparison.
Jealousy.
Children becoming entangled in their mothers' desperation for affection.
One woman crying through fertility.
Another crying through infertility.
Leah longs to be loved.
Rachel longs for children.
Even the naming of children becomes part of the emotional battlefield.
Read Genesis 29 and 30 slowly sometime.
Don't rush through the names.
Listen to the women.
There are human hearts behind those verses.
The household may contain God's covenant promises...
but it also contains tears.
Then David.
More wives.
More children.
More household complexity.
And eventually a royal family marked by horrifying sexual sin, rivalry, murder and rebellion.
We should not claim that every tragedy in David's household was mechanically caused by polygamy; Scripture itself identifies multiple sins and responsible actors.
But neither should we romanticize the structure surrounding that fractured family.
Then Solomon.
The man famous for wisdom becomes perhaps Scripture's loudest warning against confusing divine patience with divine approval.
Long before Solomon lived, Deuteronomy 17:17 warned Israel's future king:
וְלֹ֤א יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ֙ נָשִׁ֔ים
wəlōʾ yarbeh-lô nāšîm
“He shall not multiply wives for himself.”
And why?
So that his heart would not turn away.
The warning could hardly be clearer.
Then Solomon multiplied wives.
And his heart turned.
The tragedy is almost unbearable.
God had already warned Israel's kings about the danger.
Solomon's story therefore cannot honestly be used as proof that God celebrated polygamy.
It functions much more naturally as a warning.
But now we arrive at something even deeper.
Because perhaps this question isn't really just about polygamy.
Maybe underneath it is another question:
“Why does God tolerate anything He hates?”
Why did God tolerate Abraham's fear?
Jacob's deception?
David's lust?
Peter's denial?
The disciples' pride?
Your compromise?
Mine?
Suddenly this stops being an ancient theological debate.
Now it is standing in our living room.
Because it is easy to look backward at Solomon and ask:
“How could he know God's Word and still live that way?”
Until the Holy Spirit turns the mirror around.
How can we know what Jesus taught about forgiveness...
and still carry bitterness?
How can we know what Scripture teaches about purity...
and secretly feed lust?
How can we know what Christ teaches about money...
and still worship possessions?
How can we sing about surrender on Sunday...
then spend Monday negotiating which parts of our lives Jesus is actually allowed to touch?
Be careful when you ask why God tolerated sinful people in Scripture.
Because eventually you may find yourself asking why He has been so patient with you.
And that is where this story becomes breathtaking.
God's patience is not proof that sin does not matter.
God's patience is often the space in which repentance is being offered.
Tolerance is not endorsement.
Patience is not approval.
Mercy is not moral indifference.
Sometimes the terrifying thing about grace is how long God keeps calling someone who keeps running.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
You knew better.
You promised God you would stop.
Then you went back.
You deleted it.
Then downloaded it again.
You apologized.
Then repeated it.
You raised your hands in worship while carrying something inside that nobody in the room knew about.
And somewhere in the darkness you began wondering:
“Why hasn't God given up on me?”
Listen carefully.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His mercy is great.
The Gospel does not say God looked at human rebellion and decided holiness no longer mattered.
The Gospel says holiness mattered so much that the Son of God went to the cross.
Jesus does not rescue us by pretending sin is harmless.
He rescues us by bearing sin's judgment and calling sinners into a new life.
That is why the Bible's messy marriages, shattered families and scandalous failures ultimately point beyond themselves.
Humanity needed more than better rules.
We needed redemption.
And then Christ came.
The New Testament takes marriage and places it inside an astonishing Christ-centered picture.
Paul points back to Genesis' “one flesh” language in Ephesians 5 and connects marriage to Christ and the Church.
Suddenly Eden's marriage imagery reaches toward something larger.
Christ...
and His Bride.
Not a Savior exploiting His Bride.
Not a Savior abandoning His Bride when she becomes difficult.
Christ loves.
Christ gives Himself.
Christ sanctifies.
Christ remains faithful.
And this is where the Gospel becomes painfully beautiful.
Jesus is the faithful Bridegroom for an often-unfaithful people.
We wandered.
He pursued.
We sinned.
He bore the cross.
We hid.
He called us into the light.
We brought scandal.
He brought grace.
We brought guilt.
He brought forgiveness.
We brought a ruined record.
He brought His righteousness.
This is why Christianity cannot merely be reduced to “be a better person.”
The Bible contains too many broken people for that.
The message is not:
“Look how wonderful all these biblical heroes were.”
The message is:
“Look how faithful God remained in the middle of human failure.”
Abraham needed grace.
Jacob needed grace.
David needed grace.
Solomon needed grace.
Peter needed grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
And grace has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Even the New Testament's language concerning church leadership points toward marital faithfulness. In 1 Timothy 3:2 Paul uses the expression:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
mias gynaikos andra
literally, “a man/husband of one woman/wife.”

Interpreters have discussed the exact scope of that expression, so it should not be forced to carry more weight than its context permits. But at minimum, it belongs to Paul's picture of an overseer whose domestic and sexual life must be above reproach, faithful and ordered rather than characterized by uncontrolled appetite.
So why did God tolerate polygamy?
The most careful biblical answer is not, “Because God changed His mind about marriage.”
Nor should we claim more than Scripture explicitly says.
The biblical storyline is more nuanced and more powerful.

Genesis establishes the creation pattern of a man holding fast to his wife and the two becoming one flesh. Fallen humanity departs from God's good order in countless ways. The Old Testament honestly records those departures and sometimes regulates broken situations to restrain injustice and protect vulnerable people. Israel's kings are explicitly warned against multiplying wives. Jesus later points people back to what God established “from the beginning.” And the New Testament ultimately places marriage inside the magnificent picture of Christ's covenant love for His Church.
God's patience with broken human arrangements should never be mistaken for God's abandonment of His holy design.
And maybe...
just maybe...
that is the part somebody reading this desperately needed to hear.
Because you may have made choices outside God's design too.
Maybe your family story is messy.
Maybe your marriage failed.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe someone betrayed you.
Maybe sexual sin has followed you for years.
Maybe your children know a version of you that you wish you could erase.
Maybe your past contains chapters you would never post on Facebook.
And perhaps when Christians talk about God's design, all you hear is condemnation because you already know how far your life has fallen from it.
Then hear the rest of the Gospel.
Jesus does not only reveal God's standard.
Jesus receives repentant sinners.
The cross stands precisely where holiness and mercy meet.
Repentance does not mean pretending your sin never happened.
Grace means your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Bring Him the wreckage.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the relationship you destroyed.
Bring Him the shame you have polished until everyone thinks you are fine.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the scandal.
Jesus Christ specializes in resurrection.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
David was forgiven, yet consequences remained.
Choices can leave scars.
Relationships can require years of rebuilding.
Some losses cannot simply be reversed.
But scars are not the same thing as abandonment.
Consequences are not proof that grace has failed.
And your worst chapter does not possess more authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
That is why our theme at Gospel Warrior remains:
Not because scandal doesn't matter.
Because Jesus does.
Maybe this article exposed something deeper than an argument about Old Testament marriage.
Maybe somewhere between Adam, Jacob, David and Solomon...
you saw yourself.
If you did, don't hide.
And if your faith has been exhausted lately and you don't have impressive words left, simply comment, “pray for me.”
Sometimes honesty is where healing begins.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to win an argument.
Jesus already paid the price salvation required.

But if Gospel Warrior is helping you understand Scripture, encounter Christ, repent honestly and grow deeper in biblical truth, supporting and sharing this ministry is one practical way you can help put Gospel-centered teaching in front of another person who may desperately need it.
Hard questions have a way of returning.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person who has questions Christians sometimes seem afraid to answer.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks the Bible is simply a collection of perfect people pretending never to fail.
They may be surprised to discover something very different.
A book filled with deeply broken human beings...
and an astonishingly faithful God.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not leave merely knowing the answer to a theological question.
Know the Savior.
Because one day the question will not be whether Abraham had Hagar, whether Jacob married two sisters, whether David accumulated wives, or how Solomon wandered so far.
The question standing closest to eternity will be much more personal.
What did you do with Jesus?
The same Bible courageous enough to expose the scandals of its heroes is courageous enough to expose ours.
But thank God...
it does not end with scandal.
It leads us to a cross.
An empty tomb.
A risen King.
A faithful Bridegroom.
A Savior who still receives repentant sinners.
And perhaps that is the most beautiful answer of all.
God's patience with broken people was never proof that brokenness was His design; it was evidence that, even in the wreckage, He was still moving history toward the Redeemer.
And if you remember only one sentence after closing this article, remember this:
Your scandal may explain some of your scars—but it does not get to write the ending when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
